title: Embeddings
interviewAnswer: Embeddings map discrete objects such as words, products or code into dense vectors where geometry captures learned relationships. They support similarity search, retrieval and neural-network inputs.
why: Embeddings power semantic search, transformers, recommenders and graph/text systems. Interviewers expect both geometric intuition and awareness of retrieval limitations.
intuition: An embedding maps an object—word, document, image, user, PR—into a vector so that useful relationships become geometric, often measured by cosine similarity or dot product.
deepDive: Embeddings can be learned through supervised, self-supervised or contrastive objectives. Similarity reflects the training objective and domain, not universal semantic truth. Vector magnitude may carry information for dot-product retrieval; cosine normalizes it away. Retrieval systems need compatible query/document encoders, appropriate chunking and an index such as HNSW/IVF for scale.
workedExample: CodeBERT maps PR text into vectors where semantically related software changes can be closer even when they do not share exact words, which is useful for reviewer recommendation.
commonMistakes: Assuming nearest embedding means factually correct or causally related.
Mixing embeddings produced by incompatible models/spaces.
Using cosine and dot product interchangeably when vector norms differ.
followUps: How do you evaluate embedding retrieval?
production: Track embedding model/version with the index. Re-embedding can be expensive, and model changes can make old vectors incompatible with new queries.
